meta.title: Who really said "No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem"? | Quotle.info

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Washington said it in his Atlanta Exposition Address ↗ on 18 September 1895, and reprinted it in Chapter 14 of his autobiography Up from Slavery (1901). The popular wording matches the primary text word-for-word.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 18 September 1895, Cotton States and International Exposition, Atlanta

source.excerpt: Our greatest danger is that in the great leap from slavery to freedom we may overlook the fact that the masses of us are to live by the productions of our hands… No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem. It is at the bottom of life we must begin, and not at the top.
trail: The line appears verbatim in the Atlanta Exposition Address ↗, dated 18 September 1895.
It is reprinted in Chapter 14 of Up from Slavery (1901) ↗, Washington’s own account of the speech.
The speech, known as the “Atlanta Compromise ↗,” is one of the most-quoted addresses in American history.
source.excerptNote: The line comes in the passage urging his listeners to “dignify and glorify common labour.”

author.name: Booker T. Washington
author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · Educator, orator & founder of Tuskegee Institute
author.bio: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and rose to become the founding principal of the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Alabama. The most prominent Black leader in America from the 1890s until his death, he championed vocational education and economic self-reliance — a philosophy crystallized in his 1895 Atlanta Exposition Address and his best-selling autobiography Up from Slavery (1901).

misattribution.heading: Wording & attribution notes
misattribution.intro: The attribution is genuine — this really is Washington — but the line travels as a free-floating maxim, and small mis-wordings are common.

items.why: Some sites render it “No race can prosper until it learns…” The primary text reads “till it learns that there is,” per Up from Slavery, ch. 14 ↗.
The line is usually quoted with no source at all; it belongs to a specific, dated speech — the 1895 Atlanta Exposition Address ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentically Booker T. Washington, from his Atlanta Exposition Address ↗ of 18 September 1895.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Washington delivered these words to a largely white Southern audience at the Cotton States and International Exposition, framing the dignity of manual labor as the foundation of Black economic advancement. The speech became known as the “Atlanta Compromise” and made him the most influential Black spokesman of his era.

The line distills his controversial thesis: that practical, productive work carried the same worth as intellectual attainment — a stance later challenged by W. E. B. Du Bois and others who feared it conceded too much.
